subtitle: Jobs, applications, colleagues, and Feierabend
words.intro: Frankfurt calls itself Mainhattan, and its towers are full of people who have sent a German application: a photo, a signed CV, and every certificate since school.

grammar[0].blocks[2].blocks[1].text: *Feier* (celebration) + *Abend*: the end of the working day is a small party. At five, colleagues say *Schönen Feierabend!*
grammar[0].blocks[3].title: Words for the practice page
grammar[0].fact: Full-time in Germany is usually 38 to 40 hours, with at least 20 days of paid leave by law and in practice about 30. Answering work email after hours is frowned on, and in a few firms, the server simply stops delivering it.

grammar[1].blocks[0].title: They ask, you say
grammar[1].blocks[0].rows[2][1]: Ich arbeite gern im Team und bin zuverlässig.
grammar[1].blocks[0].rows[4][1]: Ja. Wie sieht ein normaler Arbeitstag aus?
grammar[1].blocks[0].note: Always have a question ready. *Nein* at the end sounds as if you do not care.
grammar[1].blocks[1].title: Words that help
grammar[1].blocks[2].title: Sie, always
grammar[1].blocks[2].text: In an interview it’s *Sie* until they offer you *du*. Some start-ups use du at once; a bank never will. If in doubt, wait and listen.
grammar[1].fact: *Der Blaue Brief*, the blue letter, is the old name for a warning or dismissal. Germans also have a *Betriebsrat*, a works council elected by staff, and in any firm above a certain size it has a real say in who gets fired.

document.intro: A real job advert from East Germany, for sailors on state cargo ships. It is fifty years old, and you could use its list for an application today: look at what it asks you to send.
document.fact: In the East, jobs like this one were sought after for a reason beyond the pay: a sailor saw the world. Not everyone got the papers to go, and the applications were read very carefully.

reading.intro: Max wants a new job, in a Frankfurt office on the 28th floor. Lena has told him the rule for German interviews: be honest, be on time, and never, ever make a joke. Frau Brandt from personnel has his application in front of her.
reading.fact: A German application traditionally includes a photo, a signed CV in table form and copies of every certificate, and a *Zeugnis* from each former employer. These are written in a secret code: *stets bemüht*, always tried hard, means useless.
